card.name: Seann Triubhas
card.tagline: A Scottish Highland dance representing the shedding of restrictive trousers for the kilt.
card.profile: The Seann Triubhas is a competitive Highland dance characterized by a transition from slow, brushing movements to rapid, high-energy steps. Its name, meaning 'old trousers' in Scottish Gaelic, is tied to narratives of cultural resistance following the 1746 Act of Proscription. Dancers perform in full Highland dress, moving through a structured sequence of slow and quick time sections.
card.insight: In 1805, Elizabeth Grant performed the dance in yellow slippers, reflecting its 19th-century history as a performance piece often taught by dancing masters.

card.profile_long: The Seann Triubhas, pronounced approximately 'shown-TROOSS', is a cornerstone of the Scottish Highland dance tradition. The name is a Scottish Gaelic phrase meaning 'old trousers'. Historically, the dance is associated with the aftermath of the Jacobite Rebellion of 1745 and the subsequent Act of Proscription in 1746, which banned the wearing of traditional Highland kilt attire. The dance is widely interpreted as a symbolic rejection of the restrictive English-style breeches that Highlanders were forced to adopt, culminating in the triumphant return to the kilt. While some traditional narratives suggest the initial slow, brushing leg movements represent the physical act of shaking off these 'despicable' trews, scholars like D. G. MacLennan have noted that these specific movements were later compositions. The dance has evolved significantly from its origins, having been taught by 19th-century dancing masters who often instructed students to perform it in regular shoes with heels. Elizabeth Grant, in her 1805 memoirs, famously recounted performing the dance in yellow slippers purchased in Perth. Today, the dance is a staple of competitive Highland dance, performed in the standard kilt outfit at events ranging from beginner categories to the premier level. The structure of the dance is highly codified, typically following either a '3 & 1' pattern (three slow steps and one quick step) or a '4 & 2' pattern (four slow steps and two quick steps). The performance begins with a mandatory opening step, after which the dancer selects from a repertoire of movements. In modern competitions, the Royal Scottish Official Board of Highland Dancing (RSOBHD) mandates specific, annually changing sequences for championship levels. The music accompanying the dance has also shifted; while it was once performed to the fiddle tune 'Seann Triubhas Uilleachan'—also known as 'The De'il Stick the Minister'—it is now almost exclusively performed to the bagpipe tune 'Whistle O'er the Lave o't'. The dance is divided into two distinct tempos: a slow section, typically ranging from 94 to 104 beats per minute, and a quick section, ranging from 112 to 124 beats per minute. The transition between these sections is signaled by the dancer clapping, which prompts the piper to accelerate the tempo. The quick-time steps share a lineage with the Highland Fling, emphasizing agility and precision. Beyond the standard competitive form, regional variants have been documented, such as the percussive style recorded in 1957 by Frank Rhodes, which was performed by Margaret Gillis in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. This version was occasionally danced to the 'Irish Washerwoman' jig. The dance remains a vital part of the Highland dance curriculum, featuring prominently in theory exams and global competitions, ensuring that the legacy of the 'old trousers' continues to be expressed through the precise, upright, and athletic movements of the modern Highland dancer.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is associated with the 1746 Act of Proscription, which banned traditional Highland dress. The name 'Seann Triubhas' translates to 'old trousers'. While popular legend links the first steps to the act of kicking off restrictive breeches, researchers like D. G. MacLennan have clarified that these steps were later additions to the tradition. The dance was historically taught by dancing masters in the 19th century and was performed in various footwear, including slippers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in either a '3 & 1' or '4 & 2' step configuration. The dance begins with a mandatory first step, followed by a series of slow, brushing movements. Upon a signal from the dancer, the music accelerates into a 'Quick Time' section, which features steps similar to the Highland Fling. The RSOBHD sets specific step requirements for championship competitions.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to the tune 'Whistle O'er the Lave o't'. Historically, it was played on the fiddle, but it is now standard to perform it to bagpipe music. The music requires a tempo shift from 94–104 bpm for the slow section to 112–124 bpm for the quick section.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear the standard Highland kilt outfit. Historically, the dance was performed in tartan trews, and in the 19th century, it was sometimes performed in regular shoes with heels.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is a primary event in global Highland dance competitions and is a standard requirement for dance theory exams. It serves as a cultural expression of the Highland identity and the historical struggle against the suppression of traditional dress.
sections.notable_figures: D. G. MacLennan, Elizabeth Grant, Margaret Gillis, Frank Rhodes, G. Douglas Taylor, William Cameron, Joan & Tom Flett.
sections.regional_variants: A percussive version was documented in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, by Frank Rhodes in 1957, which could be danced to the 'Irish Washerwoman' jig.
sections.lineage: The dance is a recognized form of Scottish Highland dance, sharing technical elements with the Highland Fling.

claims.text: The seann triubhas is a Highland dance, and is usually done in kilt.
Its name is a Scottish Gaelic phrase which means 'old trousers'.
D. G. MacLennan wrote that the first step is new to the dance and was composed by himself.
Elizabeth Grant recounted that in 1805 she danced her Shean Trews in a new pair of yellow slippers.
The dance is performed to the tune 'Whistle O'er the Lave o't'.
The dance is currently performed at most Highland dance competitions globally.
The dance is a living tradition practiced in competitions today.
